title: Why Better Product Photos Can Lift Revenue by 9.46%
summary: Etsy's buyers rank photo quality above reviews and price. What that means for your product pages, and when DIY photos stop paying for themselves.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


- In Etsy's buyer surveys, **90% of shoppers** rated photo quality as extremely or very important to a purchase decision, ahead of shipping cost, reviews and price.
- One retailer lifted revenue **9.46%** simply by making product images bigger and putting the detail within easy reach.
- Three things decide whether to shoot your own: how many products you sell, how often the range changes, and what a day of your time is worth.
- Bad photos cost you twice. Once on the sale you never make, then again on the return you pay for.
- **Snappr Pro** drops the service fee from 15% to 9% and pays for itself in roughly 4 to 6 bookings.


## Your Product Page Is a Photograph With Text Attached


When was the last time you bought something online without looking at a picture first? Probably never. The description tells you what the seller claims. The photograph is the only part of the listing that shows you.


‍


That makes product photography easy to mis-file. It looks like a design cost, so it gets treated like one and trimmed when the quarter is tight. In practice it behaves far more like stock: a fixed asset that every future sale of that product leans on. A weak photo keeps costing you for as long as the listing stays up.


Most advice here stops at "use better photos", which nobody disagrees with and nobody can act on. So here is the more useful version, in two parts. What do we actually know about photos and sales? And at what point does shooting them yourself start costing more than it saves?


## What the Evidence Actually Shows


Two numbers are worth knowing here, and both come from the people who ran the research rather than from blogs quoting each other.


‍


**Shoppers put photos ahead of reviews and price.** Etsy's seller handbook reports that in the marketplace's own buyer surveys,[90% of shoppers said photo quality was "extremely important" or "very important"](https://www.etsy.com/seller-handbook/article/147451496051) to a purchase decision, placing it ahead of shipping cost, customer reviews and the price of the item. That ordering is the surprising part. Sellers pour effort into review counts and competitive pricing, and shoppers put both of them below the photograph.


‍


**Bigger pictures sell more of the same product.** In a[VWO case study](https://vwo.com/success-stories/optimics/) , the agency Optimics tested product image treatments for the Czech retailer Mall.cz. The winning version enlarged the images and brought the product detail within easy reach, and revenue rose 9.46%. Same products, same prices, bigger pictures.


‍


Put together they describe something most sellers already half-suspect: on a product page, the photograph is doing more of the selling than the words around it.


## When DIY Photos Stop Paying for Themselves


We sell photography, which is exactly why this section is worth writing honestly. There is a real point where shooting your own stops being the cheaper option, and pretending that point sits at your very first product would not help anyone.


‍


A phone, a window and a sheet of white card will get you a perfectly good listing image. Plenty of sellers never need more than that. Three things decide when you do.


‍


**How many products you sell.** One is an afternoon. Eighty is two weeks, and the last 20 will not match the first 20, because the light shifted, your setup drifted and you got quicker as you went. Consistency across a range is the first thing in-house shooting loses, and it is the thing shoppers read as professionalism.


‍


**How often the range changes.** A single shoot is a project you can get excited about. Four a year is a standing commitment, and you pay the setup cost every time: clearing the space, rebuilding the lighting, remembering what you did last season. Seasonal sellers feel this hardest, because the shoot always lands in the week they are busiest.


‍


**What a day of your time is worth.** This is the one most people never count. A day behind the camera is a day not spent on suppliers, customers or marketing. If your time is worth $60 an hour and a full shoot swallows two days, that is around $960 gone before anyone buys a lightbox. Measured against that, commissioning starts to look cheap.


‍


Roughly where sellers land:


- **Under 20 products that rarely change.** Shoot them yourself. Spend the money somewhere it moves the needle more.
- **20 to 100, with seasonal updates.** The consistency problem starts costing more than the photos would, and you are probably already losing days you have not counted.
- **Over 100, or monthly launches.** This is a part-time job, and it is usually being done in the gaps between everything else.


‍


Your own numbers will move those lines around. The useful thing is to run the sum once, because the usual alternative is never running it and absorbing the cost for years.

## A Pre-Shoot Checklist for Online Sellers


Whether you shoot them or commission them, these are the decisions that make the difference. Most product photo problems start on the planning side rather than the camera.


- **Decide your angles once.** Front, back, side, close detail, and one shot that shows scale. Apply the same list to every product so your listings look like a range rather than a collection.
- **Always show scale.** The most common cause of a disappointed unboxing is something arriving smaller than it looked. A hand, a coin or a familiar object fixes it.
- **Shoot wide enough to crop.** Your storefront, marketplace listings, email and social all want different shapes. One generous frame beats four reshoots.
- **Go high resolution.** Shoppers zoom, and the detail is what convinces them. Shoot bigger than you think you need.
- **Keep one background.** Pick a treatment and hold it across the range. Mixed backgrounds read as mixed quality, even when each photo is good on its own.
- **Name the files properly.** Product, angle, date, applied the day they land. Nobody has ever gone back and done it later.
- **Get both the clean shot and the real one.** A cut-out tells shoppers what it is. A photo of it in use tells them what owning it feels like. Most listings want both.


## The Cost of Bad Product Photography


The downside is easier to measure than the upside, and it makes the more convincing case.


‍


A weak photo does not just fail to convert. It quietly filters traffic you already paid for through ads, search or marketplace fees. That impression costs you the same whether the photo works or not.


‍


Then there is the return, which is where it gets expensive. When something arrives looking different from its listing, you lose:


- The margin on the sale, plus return shipping and handling.
- The item as new stock, since most returns cannot go back on the shelf at full price.
- Listing visibility, because marketplaces read high return rates as a quality problem and push you down.
- The customer, who rarely comes back after returning something.


‍


So one avoidable return is never one lost sale. On a 20% margin you need several clean orders to cover it. That makes honest photography a profit question rather than a styling one, and it is why showing true color, texture and scale beats making the product look better than it is.
